claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoparticles have a fully random, disordered atomic configuration.
Annealing at 700–900 °C can selectively increase atomic short-range order in these nanoparticles.
The proposed annealing treatment can increase short-range order without causing grain growth or morphological changes.
High-resolution diffraction and pair distribution function analysis can verify that local ordering is the only structural variable modified by annealing.
Enhanced local atomic short-range order produces regions of increased lattice strain.
Enhanced local atomic short-range order produces heterogeneous bond energies.
Annealing-induced atomic rearrangements create localized strained regions at the nanoparticle surface.
Localized lattice strain weakens cohesive bonds at the nanoparticle surface.
Weaker surface cohesive bonds lower the activation barrier or activation temperature for surface-atom mobility.
Lowering the barrier for surface-atom mobility causes an earlier onset of surface premelting.
Annealed nanoparticles will have a statistically significant lower surface-premelting onset temperature than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
The overall bulk melting point will remain largely unchanged after annealing.
The as-synthesized baseline has a higher surface-premelting temperature threshold than the annealed nanoparticles.
The proposed ordering effect should operate from just below the baseline premelting onset through complete melting.
Using narrow, matched nanoparticle size distributions makes size effects minimal.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field correctly describes annealing-induced grain growth or morphology changes as confounders, whereas the falsification rule treats their occurrence as falsifying the short-range-order mechanism. Such changes would make the comparison non-controlled and therefore inconclusive rather than directly falsifying the mechanism.
